nameStory: Red amaranth gets its colorful name from the deep crimson and burgundy hues that often tinge its stems, leaves, and especially its dense flower clusters. The word 'amaranth' comes from the Greek 'amarantos,' meaning 'unfading' or 'everlasting,' referring to how the papery flowers retain their color long after drying.
description: Red amaranth is a tall, sturdy annual plant that can reach 3-6 feet in height with a robust, upright growth habit. This cultivated grain crop has escaped gardens to grow wild in some areas of New England. Its most striking feature is the dense, upright cluster of tiny flowers that forms a thick, fuzzy-looking spike at the top of the plant, often tinged with red or purple colors. The whole plant has a substantial, almost shrub-like appearance when mature.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, upright flower spikes that feel soft and velvety to the touch, packed with countless tiny flowers that lack petals but have colorful sepals ranging from green to deep red

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately on the stem, often with reddish veins or tinges, feeling smooth but substantial between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, robust annual that stands very upright with thick, sturdy stems that may have a reddish cast, creating an almost shrub-like silhouette

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, shiny black or dark brown seeds that feel hard and bead-like, contained in small capsules that split open when mature

habitat: Red amaranth thrives in disturbed, nutrient-rich soils and is most commonly found in gardens, farmyards, vacant lots, and along roadsides where the soil has been cultivated or enriched. It prefers full sun and well-drained soil, often appearing as an escape from cultivation rather than a truly wild plant. You'll typically find it in areas with human activity rather than deep in the woods.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with the first warm weather, showing their characteristic oval leaves with possible reddish tinges.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly and begin producing their distinctive upright flower spikes by mid to late summer, when they're most easily identified.
seasonality.fall: Flower spikes mature and produce abundant seeds, while the whole plant may take on more pronounced red and purple coloring before frost kills it.
seasonality.winter: This annual plant dies completely with frost, leaving only dried stalks and scattered seeds that may germinate the following spring.

funFact: The tiny seeds of red amaranth were so important to the Aztecs that they mixed them with honey and human blood to create ceremonial sculptures of their gods - a practice so alarming to Spanish conquistadors that they banned amaranth cultivation entirely, nearly driving this ancient superfood to extinction.
confusionNotes: Red amaranth is most easily confused with love-lies-bleeding, its close cousin, but love-lies-bleeding has long, drooping, rope-like flower clusters that hang down like tassels, while red amaranth's flowers stand stiffly upright like thick candles.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'red' amaranth, the red coloring can vary greatly - some plants may be mostly green while others are deeply burgundy. This is actually an ancient grain crop that's been cultivated for thousands of years, so finding it growing wild usually means it has escaped from someone's garden rather than being truly native to the area.
compareHints: Among its amaranth relatives, red amaranth stands out for its particularly robust, upright growth and thick, erect flower spikes. Unlike the drooping clusters of love-lies-bleeding or the sprawling habit of redroot amaranth, red amaranth maintains a very vertical, almost architectural appearance. Its flowers are also typically more densely packed and substantial-looking than most of its weedy cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England amaranths, redroot is distinguished by its reddish taproot and compact, bristly flower clusters.
Unlike the weedy Redroot Amaranth found in gardens and fields, Tidalmarsh Amaranth is strictly a coastal specialist that grows much taller and in dense colonies.

Purple amaranth stands out from its amaranth relatives by its distinctly prostrate, mat-forming growth habit - while redroot amaranth and smooth pigweed grow upright like small bushes, purple amaranth sprawls along the ground.
Love-lies-bleeding stands out dramatically from its wild amaranth relatives in New England because of its long, pendulous flower clusters - all the others have upright, spike-like flower heads.
Compared to redroot amaranth, smooth pigweed has less hairy stems and leaves, and its flower spikes tend to be more upright rather than drooping.
Among the New England amaranths, rough-fruit amaranth stands out for its preference for wetter habitats and its distinctively bumpy seeds.
Among New England's amaranths, green amaranth is unique for maintaining its green color throughout the season - most others develop reddish or purplish tones in stems, roots, or flower clusters.
Among New England's amaranths, spiny amaranth is the only one with actual spines - species like redroot amaranth and smooth pigweed may have bristly flowers but lack the sharp spines at leaf bases.
Palmer's Amaranth stands out from its amaranth relatives because it's 'dioecious' - meaning individual plants are either male or female, not both like most other amaranths.
Powell's amaranth differs from redroot amaranth by lacking the red-tinged roots and having less hairy leaves.
Unlike its weedy cousins like Redroot Amaranth that grow tall and upright in disturbed soils, Seabeach Amaranth stays flat against the sand and has much thicker, more succulent leaves and stems.
